title: Data Contamination & Trustworthy Evaluation
summary: Audit how evaluation information could reach training or model selection. Separate literal overlap, semantic exposure, and adaptive benchmark reuse, and design an evaluation protocol whose uncertainty claims remain interpretable.
intuition: A benchmark is meant to stand in for unseen problems. If the training process has seen the same problem, a paraphrase, its solution, or repeated feedback about that benchmark, a high score can reflect exposure rather than transferable skill. Exact matching provides strong evidence of a particular kind of overlap, but zero exact matches does not prove an uncontaminated evaluation. Conversely, a model assigning high likelihood to text is not proof that it trained on that text.
math: Overlap=|E ∩ T|/|E|; Jaccard(A,B)=|A∩B|/|A∪B|; observed score=(1-c)·clean score+c·exposed score for a specified mixture.
derivation:
1. Define the intended generalization unit: a document, patient, code repository, problem family, or future time period. This determines what must remain separate across training, tuning, and evaluation.
2. Build provenance records for data versions, source groups, timestamps, preprocessing, and model-selection access. Contamination is a path of information flow, not just one duplicate-text test.
3. Normalize only transformations that preserve the intended identity, then hash for exact matches. Keep raw data and the normalization policy because aggressive normalization can create false equivalences. Hash matches should lead to inspectable source records.
4. For candidate near-duplicates, compare text shingles or embeddings and manually audit representative matches. Jaccard similarity of shingle sets is $|A\cap B|/|A\cup B|$. A threshold is an engineering choice whose false-positive and false-negative rates must be checked on the relevant domain.
5. Group connected duplicate families before splitting. Deduplicating each split separately can leave one copy of the same family in train and test. Code repositories, patients, and templated tasks may require grouping even without high lexical overlap.
6. A toy evaluation mixture with exposed fraction c satisfies $s_{\mathrm{obs}}=(1-c)s_{\mathrm{clean}}+cs_{\mathrm{exposed}}$ when these subgroup scores and weights are well defined. This arithmetic illustrates distortion; unknown membership and unknown subgroup effects do not provide an automatic decontamination correction.
7. Closed training corpora make direct overlap audits incomplete. Membership-inference or likelihood-based detectors provide model-dependent evidence, not definitive membership labels; distribution and temporal shifts can confound their evaluation. Report uncertainty and detection coverage.
8. Freeze a final holdout after tuning decisions, restrict its access, and evaluate fresh or temporally separated tasks when appropriate. Report overlap policies and sensitivity results alongside benchmark scores. A temporal split also changes the target distribution and does not by itself rule out copied or paraphrased content.
application: Audit pretrained-model evaluations, construct leakage-resistant code and document splits, investigate surprising benchmark gains, and record what a contamination detector can actually establish. Pair exact-match evidence with group provenance and fresh held-out evaluation rather than interpreting a single similarity threshold as a clean bill of health.
mistakes: Treating zero exact hash collisions as proof that no contamination exists
Deduplicating within each split but not across splits
Using a likelihood-based membership detector as ground truth
Removing only poorly performing contaminated items after seeing scores
Ignoring repeated benchmark feedback during prompt or hyperparameter tuning
interview: I would define the independence unit and map every route from evaluation into training or selection. Then I would audit exact overlap, near-duplicates, groups, and temporal provenance, documenting detector limitations. I would reserve an untouched final evaluation and report how performance changes under defensible exclusion policies.
followUps: How can adaptive benchmark reuse leak information without any example appearing in training text?
What ground truth and controls are needed to evaluate a membership-inference detector?
Why might a time-based split change both contamination risk and task difficulty?

title: Contrastive Learning & Representation Geometry
summary: Learn embeddings by identifying matching views among alternatives. Connect the classification-style loss to its gradients, the geometry of normalized representations, and the assumptions hidden in data augmentation.
intuition: Treat one augmented view as a query and ask which candidate came from the same example. Pulling the match closer is only half the task: the denominator also compares it with competing views. What counts as a matching view defines what information the representation is encouraged to retain.
derivation:
1. Encode two independently augmented views of each of $N$ examples. A batch contains $2N$ embeddings; each anchor has one paired positive and $2N-2$ other candidates. Exclude the anchor itself, but keep its positive in the denominator.
2. Normalize embeddings and define similarity $s_{ij}=u_i^\top u_j$. Divide similarities by a positive temperature $\tau$ to obtain logits.
3. This is a categorical classification problem: identify the positive among candidates. Expanding negative log probability gives $\ell_i=-s_{i+}/\tau+\log\sum_{j\ne i}\exp(s_{ij}/\tau)$.
4. Differentiate with respect to a similarity: $\partial\ell_i/\partial s_{ij}=(p_{ij}-\mathbf1[j=+])/\tau$. A high-scoring negative receives a larger repulsive contribution. The positive receives an attractive contribution unless its predicted probability is already 1.
5. If $u=z/\|z\|_2$, normalization has Jacobian $(I-uu^\top)/\|z\|_2$ for nonzero $z$. This projects gradient onto directions tangent to the unit sphere; normalized similarity is not increased merely by scaling the vector.
6. Decreasing temperature changes both the probability distribution and the explicit gradient scale. It emphasizes hard competitors but may amplify noisy or false-negative comparisons.
7. Low training loss does not prove useful semantic features. If an augmentation removes the task label or if many negatives are actually equivalent, the training task can conflict with the desired representation. Evaluate frozen features, transfer, and augmentation ablations.
application: Use this framework for image representations, paired image–text retrieval, and matching embeddings. A learned projection head may absorb invariances useful for the contrastive objective; evaluate whether downstream tasks should use encoder features or projected features rather than assuming they are interchangeable.
mistakes: Leaving the anchor's self-similarity in the denominator
Assuming all different examples are semantically negative
Treating temperature only as a gradient multiplier
Using label-changing augmentations without checking the downstream task
interview: A contrastive loss classifies the matching view among alternatives. Its gradient increases relative positive similarity and decreases competing similarities. The difficult design questions are what constitutes a positive, how negatives are sampled, and whether the induced invariances preserve the downstream information.
code:
import numpy as np
def paired_contrastive_loss(z, temperature=0.2):
    # Order: first views [0:N], matching second views [N:2N].
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    if z.ndim != 2 or len(z) < 4 or len(z) % 2:
        raise ValueError("an even batch with at least two pairs is required")
    if temperature <= 0:
        raise ValueError("temperature must be positive")
    norms = np.linalg.norm(z, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    if np.any(norms == 0):
        raise ValueError("zero embeddings cannot be normalized")
    u = z / norms
    logits = (u @ u.T) / temperature
    np.fill_diagonal(logits, -np.inf)
    m = logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    log_denom = m[:, 0] + np.log(np.exp(logits-m).sum(axis=1))
    n = len(z)//2
    positive = (np.arange(2*n) + n) % (2*n)
    return np.mean(log_denom - logits[np.arange(2*n), positive])
followUps: Why might encoder features transfer better than projection-head outputs?
How can false negatives change the gradient for a semantically correct neighbor?

title: Diffusion Models: Noise, Denoising & Sampling
summary: Derive the directly sampled noisy input, understand what a noise-prediction network learns, and separate a training objective from a reverse-time sampling algorithm.
intuition: We know how to gradually corrupt data with Gaussian noise. Training provides a noisy observation and its noise level, then asks a network to estimate the corruption. Generation starts from noise and uses a sequence of learned denoising steps; predicting a clean sample once is not automatically the same as sampling the reverse process.
derivation:
1. Choose variances $0<\beta_t<1$ and write $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$. The forward transition is $x_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\epsilon_t$ with independent standard Gaussian noise.
2. Substituting earlier steps gives a coefficient $\sqrt{\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s}$ on the original data. Independent Gaussian noise terms add in variance.
3. If accumulated noise variance at step $t-1$ is $1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$, the next variance is $\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})+\beta_t=1-\bar\alpha_t$. This proves the closed-form noisy sample and avoids simulating all earlier steps during training.
4. Sample a time $t$ and noise $\epsilon$, create $x_t$, and minimize $\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2$. Under squared error, the population optimum is the conditional mean $\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t,t]$, not recovery of every sample's exact hidden noise.
5. Rearranging the forward equation yields $\hat x_0=(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon_\theta)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$. When $\bar\alpha_t$ is tiny, a small noise-prediction error can imply a large clean-sample error.
6. A DDPM reverse mean can be parameterized as $\mu_\theta=\alpha_t^{-1/2}(x_t-\beta_t\epsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t})$. A sampling step also needs a variance choice and noise for nonfinal steps. Do not substitute the clean-sample estimate for the entire reverse transition.
7. The common unweighted noise-MSE objective is a useful training objective, not literally every term and weighting in a full variational bound. State the parameterization and timestep weighting when comparing objectives.
application: Apply these ideas to image, audio, and latent-space generation. Debug data scaling, noise schedules, timestep conditioning, and reverse-step indexing before attributing poor samples solely to architecture. Assess quality, diversity, and sampling cost together.
mistakes: Using alpha_t where cumulative alpha-bar_t is required
Forgetting timestep conditioning
Assuming the predicted noise equals the exact hidden draw for every example
Injecting reverse-process noise into a final step that should be deterministic
interview: A diffusion model learns denoising across known noise levels. The forward process has a closed-form Gaussian marginal, making training efficient. Reverse generation uses a learned mean plus a specified variance schedule; the loss parameterization and sampler are separate design choices.
followUps: Why does the choice of timestep weighting change which noise levels dominate training?
How do deterministic and stochastic samplers differ even with the same trained model?

title: Mixture of Experts: Routing, Capacity & Balance
summary: Separate total parameters from active per-token computation. Trace tokens through a router and experts, and reason about capacity, gradient flow, and distributed communication.
intuition: A token does not necessarily need every specialist network. A router selects a few experts and combines their outputs. The savings in arithmetic can be lost if routing overloads one expert or requires expensive data movement.
derivation:
1. Replace a dense feed-forward block with $E$ expert networks and a router. Router logits $r(x)$ produce probabilities $p=\operatorname{softmax}(r(x))$.
2. Select the top $k$ experts. The displayed mixture normalizes probabilities over the selected set, then forms a weighted sum. Other implementations keep unnormalized selected gate values; these conventions are not interchangeable.
3. If each expert has $P$ parameters, expert storage is roughly $EP$, while selected expert computation per token is roughly $k$ times one expert's work. Shared layers and the router are additional. Every expert can still require storage even if only a few are active for a given token.
4. With $T$ tokens, top-k routing creates $kT$ assignments. Average assignment count per expert is $kT/E$. A capacity factor $c$ gives a planning capacity $C=\lceil ckT/E\rceil$. Actual maxima can exceed this average-based allowance.
5. Count routed assignments and specify an overflow policy: drop, reroute, queue, or use a dropless implementation. Dropping a branch must have a defined interaction with the residual path and mixture normalization.
6. For top-1 Switch-style balancing, let $f_e$ be the observed fraction of tokens sent to expert e and $P_e$ the average soft router probability. An auxiliary term proportional to $E\sum_e f_eP_e$ encourages alignment with balanced usage; the discrete counts are not ordinary differentiable routing decisions.
7. A subtle edge case: if top-1 gates are renormalized over the singleton set, their weight becomes 1. The task loss has no continuous gradient through that weight to the router. Router learning then needs another path or objective. Keeping the selected soft gate value changes this behavior.
8. In expert parallelism, tokens are dispatched to devices and results returned. Account for all-to-all bandwidth, padding, small per-expert batches, and load imbalance when judging end-to-end efficiency.
application: Use sparse experts when increasing model capacity while controlling per-token arithmetic is valuable. Compare quality at matched active FLOPs, total memory, batch/sequence shape, and network topology. Active parameter count alone is not a latency prediction.
mistakes: Equating active parameters with total stored parameters
Ignoring expert overload and dropped tokens
Assuming hard top-k selection is differentiable everywhere
Renormalizing top-1 gates without considering router gradients
interview: MoE trades sparse computation for routing complexity. A small set of experts processes each token, but all expert weights still exist. The central engineering questions are load balance, capacity and overflow policy, communication, and whether the router receives a useful learning signal.
code:
import numpy as np
def route_topk(logits, k, capacity):
    # Educational routing plan: normalized selected gates, explicit overflow mask.
    logits = np.asarray(logits, float)
    tokens, experts = logits.shape
    if not 1 <= k <= experts or capacity < 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid k or capacity")
    ids = np.argsort(-logits, axis=1, kind="stable")[:, :k]
    selected = np.take_along_axis(logits, ids, axis=1)
    weights = np.exp(selected-selected.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    weights /= weights.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    counts = np.zeros(experts, dtype=int)
    accepted = np.zeros((tokens, k), dtype=bool)
    for t in range(tokens):
        for slot, e in enumerate(ids[t]):
            accepted[t, slot] = counts[e] < capacity
            counts[e] += 1
    # Rejected branches contribute zero; weights are NOT renormalized afterward.
    return ids, weights*accepted, accepted, counts
followUps: When is a dropless implementation preferable to a fixed-capacity kernel?
How can routing imbalance change as the deployment distribution shifts?

title: Long Context: Position, Memory & Evidence Use
summary: Distinguish accepting a long input, computing attention efficiently, and using distant evidence correctly. Connect position encoding, prefill complexity, cache growth, and controlled evaluation.
intuition: A larger desk lets you spread out more pages, but does not guarantee that you find and combine the right facts. Long-context engineering must preserve positional behavior, fit memory budgets, and demonstrate evidence use rather than merely successful execution.
derivation:
1. During prefill, each query attends to many key positions. Dense attention uses a score matrix with $T^2$ entries per head and quadratic attention arithmetic. Doubling T multiplies this component by about four; it does not necessarily quadruple the entire model's runtime.
2. During cached decoding, old keys and values are reused. Per layer, each token contributes $H_{\mathrm{kv}}d_h$ key elements and the same number of value elements. Multiplying by layers, batch, length and element size gives the KV-memory formula.
3. Efficient exact-attention kernels can avoid materializing the full score matrix and reduce memory traffic. That does not turn the underlying dense attention arithmetic into linear complexity.
4. Rotary position embedding rotates coordinate pairs. In a two-dimensional block, $(R(m\theta)q)^\top R(n\theta)k=q^\top R((n-m)\theta)k$. Thus relative displacement enters the attention dot product through a rotation.
5. This algebraic relative-position property does not guarantee extrapolation beyond training lengths. At unseen displacements the model can encounter phase patterns and evidence configurations it did not learn to use.
6. Extending context can involve positional rescaling, long-sequence training, architectural sparsity, or retrieval. Specify which mechanism changed and compare quality and cost at matched budgets.
7. Evaluate multiple lengths, evidence positions, distractor counts, and tasks requiring one versus several pieces of evidence. Include counterfactual evidence that changes the answer, oracle retrieval, and contamination controls.
8. Separate successful allocation, exact retrieval, evidence synthesis, and refusal when evidence is missing. Measure TTFT and memory alongside answer quality rather than collapsing all results into one long-context score.
application: Use this analysis for document QA, code repositories, long conversations, and large-context serving. It helps distinguish a position-encoding bug from a retrieval failure or a memory bottleneck.
mistakes: Treating the advertised maximum input length as a capability guarantee
Claiming FlashAttention makes dense attention linear-time
Using query-head count instead of KV-head count in GQA cache estimates

title: Reinforcement Learning: Returns, Bellman Equations & TD
summary: Build a precise model of sequential decisions, derive the value recursion, and implement a small temporal-difference update. Distinguish the policy being evaluated from the policy being improved.
intuition: An action can have a small immediate reward but open a valuable future. A value function estimates that future, while a policy chooses actions. Learning is difficult because the policy changes which data it sees and because the consequences of an action may arrive much later.
derivation:
1. In an MDP, the distribution of the next state and reward depends on the current state and action. A partial observation need not be a Markov state; history or memory may be required.
2. Split the discounted return into the first reward and the rest: $G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}$. Taking conditional expectations under a fixed policy gives $V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\mathbb E[R_{t+1}+\gamma V^\pi(S_{t+1})\mid s,a]$.
3. For a finite MDP and fixed policy, write $V=r_\pi+\gamma P_\pi V$. When $\gamma<1$, $V=(I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}r_\pi$, though iterative methods avoid explicitly inverting a large matrix.
4. The Bellman expectation operator contracts sup-norm differences by at most $\gamma$, since a probability-weighted average cannot exceed the maximum difference. This gives a unique fixed point for discounted tabular policy evaluation.
5. A sample transition replaces the expectation with a noisy target. TD(0) uses $\delta=r+\gamma V(s')-V(s)$ and $V(s)\leftarrow V(s)+\eta\delta$. At a true terminal state, omit the future-value term.
6. Q-learning instead targets $r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$. The behavior policy can explore while the update targets a greedy policy, making it off-policy. SARSA uses the actually selected next action and is on-policy.
7. An externally imposed time limit is not automatically a terminal state of the underlying task. If the task continues, bootstrap from the final observation at truncation; if a finite horizon defines the task, include remaining time in the state and use appropriate terminal semantics.
8. Tabular convergence guarantees require assumptions such as sufficient visitation and suitable step sizes. They do not automatically transfer to nonlinear function approximation, changing data distributions, or arbitrary replay schemes.
application: These ideas support control, recommendation with delayed outcomes, and policy optimization in modern AI. Before choosing an algorithm, define reward timing, episode boundaries, available state, exploration, and the evaluation distribution.

Treating a partial observation as a guaranteed Markov state

Zeroing the bootstrap for every time-limit truncation
Applying tabular guarantees unchanged to deep networks
interview: RL optimizes expected return under a policy that influences the future data distribution. Bellman equations express a long-horizon value as one reward plus discounted future value. TD learns from sampled transitions; Q-learning evaluates a greedy target even when behavior explores.

    target = reward + gamma*bootstrap

title: Speech Alignment with Connectionist Temporal Classification
summary: Train a frame-level sequence model from a transcript without frame-by-frame alignments. Understand how CTC sums valid alignments and why blank handling, repeated characters, and sequence lengths matter.
intuition: Many frame sequences can express the same transcript: a sound can span several frames and silence need not emit a label. CTC assigns probability to all paths that collapse to the transcript rather than demanding one known timing alignment.
math: $$P(y\mid x)=\sum_{\pi:B(\pi)=y}\prod_{t=1}^T p_t(\pi_t\mid x),\qquad L=-\log P(y\mid x).$$
derivation:
1. At each of T encoder frames, predict probabilities over labels plus a special blank. The encoder may use temporal context; the CTC path probability still factorizes over output frames conditional on the input.
2. Define collapse B by merging consecutive identical symbols first, then removing blanks. The path (a,a,blank,a) becomes aa, not a. A blank can separate two occurrences of the same label.
3. Sum probabilities of every path that collapses to the target. Maximizing only one alignment changes the objective and discards uncertainty about timing.
4. For target labels $(y_1,\ldots,y_U)$, insert blanks to form $z=(blank,y_1,blank,\ldots,y_U,blank)$. Let $A_t(s)$ be the total path probability reaching extended position s at frame t.
5. A path can stay at s or advance from s−1. It can skip from s−2 only if z_s is not blank and differs from z_{s-2}; otherwise it would merge distinct required repetitions.
6. Multiply the sum of allowed predecessor probabilities by $p_t(z_s)$. Initialize only the first blank and first label at frame 1; finish by summing the last label and last blank states.
7. The dynamic program costs $O(TU)$ instead of enumerating exponentially many paths. Use log probabilities and log-sum-exp for realistic sequence lengths.
8. A target with U labels and R adjacent repeated-label pairs requires at least U+R frames. Greedy frame argmax followed by collapse need not maximize transcript probability, because multiple lower-probability paths may combine into a stronger transcript.
application: Use CTC for speech recognition or handwriting when inputs are longer than output labels and alignments are monotonic. Check the encoder's subsampled frame lengths and blank convention. Attention-based and transducer objectives make different dependency assumptions.
mistakes: Removing blanks before merging repeats
Treating blank as a literal space in the transcript
Passing probabilities where a loss API expects log probabilities
Ignoring repeated-label minimum lengths
Assuming the most likely path gives the most likely transcript
interview: CTC marginalizes over monotonic frame-to-label alignments. A blank and a collapse rule represent repeated frames and timing gaps. A forward dynamic program sums valid paths, including special restrictions for repeated labels; greedy path decoding is only an approximation to transcript-level decoding.
followUps: How does encoder time subsampling affect the feasibility of repeated-label targets?

title: Disjoint Sets: Connectivity Without Repeated Traversal
summary: Maintain an evolving partition when edges arrive incrementally. Derive the tree-height invariant, implement union by size with path compression, and explain why deletions require another approach.
intuition: A representative is a label for a whole connected component, not a graph center. Linking two representatives merges all members without updating each member immediately. A find operation can shorten the route to that label.

title: Dynamic Programming: State Design and Safe Memory Compression
summary: Design a state that summarizes the past, derive transitions by an exhaustive case split, and compress memory without changing the problem being solved.
intuition: A DP table is a collection of small, precisely defined questions. Memoization only helps after those questions preserve all information needed by future choices. The loop order determines which version of a state an update reads.
derivation: For 0/1 knapsack, define $D_i(c)$ as the best value using only the first i items with total weight at most c. Partition feasible solutions by whether item i is absent or present. The absent case gives $D_{i-1}(c)$; the present case reserves its weight and adds its value to $D_{i-1}(c-w_i)$. These cases are exhaustive and disjoint, proving the recurrence by induction from $D_0(c)=0$. Compressing to one array is safe only if capacities are visited in descending order: the lower-capacity entry still belongs to the previous item row. Ascending updates may reuse the same item, silently solving an unbounded variant. Complexity is $O(nC)$, pseudo-polynomial in numeric capacity C rather than its bit length.

Calling O(nC) polynomial in the encoded input size

summary: Build a transparent single-channel 2D convolution reference, then derive its backward pass by following each output’s dependence on an input patch.
intuition: A shared kernel scores every local patch. Sharing means a kernel parameter receives gradient contributions from many positions. Overlap means an input pixel can receive gradients from several outputs, so backward must accumulate.

title: Build a Tiny Reverse-Mode Autograd Engine
summary: Implement scalar reverse-mode differentiation with a computation graph, local backward rules, and correct handling of a value reused along several paths.
intuition: Every operation stores a small promise: if I later receive a derivative with respect to my output, I can distribute derivatives to my inputs. Reverse topological order ensures all downstream contributions arrive before that promise is executed.
derivation: For an operation $v=f(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$ and adjoint $\bar v=\partial L/\partial v$, the chain rule sends $\bar v\,\partial v/\partial u_j$ to each input. A reused input receives a sum over every outgoing use, including two positions in the same operation. Topological traversal should visit a node once, but the local rule must preserve operand multiplicity. For $a=x x$ and $L=a+a x$, the derivative reaching a is $1+x$, and x also receives the direct contribution a. Therefore $dL/dx=2x(1+x)+x^2=2x+3x^2$. At x=2 it is 16. A depth-first postorder followed in reverse computes this exactly. The educational engine resets all reachable adjoints on each backward call; this intentionally differs from PyTorch leaf-gradient accumulation across backward calls.
application: Reverse mode efficiently differentiates one scalar loss with respect to many parameters without constructing a dense Jacobian. The same graph reasoning explains detached tensors, repeated backward calls, and why in-place changes to saved forward values can invalidate gradients.

class Value:
    def __init__(self, data, parents=()):
        self.data = float(data); self.grad = 0.0
        self.parents = parents; self._backward = lambda: None
    def __add__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data + other.data, (self, other))
        def rule():
            self.grad += out.grad
            other.grad += out.grad
        out._backward = rule
        return out
    def __mul__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other))
        left, right = self.data, other.data  # save forward values
        def rule():
            self.grad += right * out.grad
            other.grad += left * out.grad
        out._backward = rule
        return out
    def backward(self):
        order, seen = [], set()
        def visit(node):
            if node in seen: return
            seen.add(node)
            for parent in node.parents: visit(parent)
            order.append(node)
        visit(self)
        for node in order: node.grad = 0.0
        self.grad = 1.0
        for node in reversed(order): node._backward()

title: Activation Checkpointing: Recompute Instead of Retain
summary: Derive a simple memory model for segmented checkpointing, implement recomputation on a scalar network, and separate activation savings from parameters, gradients, and optimizer state.
intuition: Backward needs selected forward values, not necessarily every value stored for the whole step. Save a few boundary activations, then replay a segment when its gradients are needed. You buy memory with additional arithmetic and careful control of state.
derivation: Consider L equal-sized sequential layers and checkpoint every s layers. Retain roughly L/s boundary activations. During backward, replay one segment and retain its s local activations temporarily. Ignoring endpoints and workspaces, peak saved activation units are $L/s+s$. Differentiating this continuous estimate gives $1-L/s^2=0$, so $s\approx\sqrt L$ minimizes the model. This is an intuition under uniform layers, not an exact optimizer for transformer memory. Replay preserves gradients only if it reconstructs the same needed values: random masks, mutation, and side effects matter. Parameters and optimizer states still exist; recomputation cannot remove their memory. The reference chain uses deterministic tanh layers and recomputes every segment once, adding one extra forward traversal while avoiding persistent storage of all intermediates.
application: Checkpoint large activation-heavy blocks when memory, rather than parameter storage, limits batch size or context. Profile actual peak allocated memory and step time. Compare the same batch, seed, precision, and model before attributing a throughput change to checkpointing alone.
mistakes: Confusing activation checkpointing with saving a training checkpoint to disk
Predicting total GPU memory from activation units alone
Replaying a different dropout mask
Allowing stateful counters or running statistics to update twice
interview: I retain segment inputs and reconstruct local intermediates during backward. This trades extra forward work for lower activation memory. I verify gradient equivalence and check RNG and side effects; the savings depend on the model’s actual memory breakdown.
code:
from math import tanh

def checkpoint_chain(x, weights, segment):
    if segment < 1: raise ValueError('segment must be positive')
    saved = {0: x}; y = x
    for i,w in enumerate(weights, 1):
        y = tanh(w*y)
        if i % segment == 0 or i == len(weights): saved[i] = y
    edges = sorted(saved)
    dw = [0.0]*len(weights); upstream = 1.0
    for block in range(len(edges)-1, 0, -1):
        start, end = edges[block-1], edges[block]
        local = [saved[start]]
        for i in range(start,end):
            local.append(tanh(weights[i]*local[-1]))
        for i in range(end-1,start-1,-1):
            offset = i-start
            dz = upstream*(1-local[offset+1]**2)
            dw[i] = dz*local[offset]
            upstream = dz*weights[i]
    return y, upstream, dw

weights = [0.9,1.1,0.8,1.2,0.7]
y, dx, dw = checkpoint_chain(0.4, weights, 2)
def forward(x, ws):
    for w in ws: x = tanh(w*x)
    return x
eps = 1e-5
assert abs(dx-(forward(.4+eps,weights)-forward(.4-eps,weights))/(2*eps)) < 1e-8
for i,w in enumerate(weights):
    weights[i]=w+eps; hi=forward(.4,weights)
    weights[i]=w-eps; lo=forward(.4,weights)
    weights[i]=w
    assert abs(dw[i]-(hi-lo)/(2*eps)) < 1e-8
assert checkpoint_chain(.4, weights, 1) == checkpoint_chain(.4, weights, 2)

title: Collective Communication: What Moves, Who Receives It
summary: Distinguish collective semantics from transport algorithms, calculate a ring all-reduce estimate, and derive correct gradient weighting when ranks process different sample counts.
intuition: First ask what each rank must know after the operation. All-reduce replicates a reduction everywhere; reduce-scatter gives each rank one reduced shard; all-gather reconstructs the full set of shards. These describe outputs, not a mandatory network topology.
derivation: Partition an N-byte vector evenly across p ranks. An idealized ring reduce-scatter uses p−1 rounds, each sending N/p bytes per rank; all-gather uses another p−1 rounds. With latency alpha per round and bandwidth B, the model is $2(p-1)\alpha+2(p-1)N/(pB)$. It ignores overlap, topology bottlenecks, and software effects; small messages can be latency dominated even when bandwidth is high. For training, if rank r averages over n_r examples, its local mean gradient g_r must be weighted by n_r before summation and divided by total examples. Averaging rank means equally is correct only when those counts match, or when equal weighting of ranks is the intended objective. Every participant must execute compatible collectives in a consistent order.
application: Data-parallel training uses gradient reduction, while sharded optimizers can retain reduce-scattered shards instead of immediately reconstructing full gradients. Tensor parallelism and expert routing need different communication patterns. Estimate bytes and synchronization latency before changing bucket size, then confirm with a trace.
mistakes: Confusing all-gather with summing vectors
Assuming summed gradients are automatically averaged
Averaging unequal-sized batch means equally
Skipping a collective on one rank after a conditional branch
Treating the ring model as a measured latency prediction
interview: I specify input and output ownership before choosing a collective. Reduce-scatter plus all-gather can implement all-reduce. I estimate payload and synchronization cost separately, and derive gradient normalization from the sample counts rather than assuming equal batches.
followUps: When does reducing bucket size improve overlap but increase overhead?
Why does asynchronous launch not guarantee that computation and communication overlap?
